passed.title: Expr.shrink_dtype is a deprecated no-op
passed.trap: Since 1.33.0, `Expr.shrink_dtype` is deprecated and does nothing. Calling it emits a deprecation warning and leaves the dtype unchanged, so any memory saving you expected never happens. Use `Series.shrink_dtype` on materialized data instead, for example via `DataFrame.get_column`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import warnings

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    via_expr = df.select(pl.col("a").shrink_dtype())
print(via_expr.dtypes)  # [Int64] - unchanged
via_series = df.get_column("a").shrink_dtype()
print(via_series.dtype)  # Int8

passed.title: Sum of an all-null or empty column is 0, not null
passed.trap: `Expr.sum` returns `0` when there are no non-null values, unlike SQL `SUM`, which returns NULL. In a `DataFrame.group_by` aggregation, a group whose values are all missing silently reports a total of 0, which looks the same as a real zero. Aggregate `Expr.count` next to the sum so empty groups can be detected. If an empty sum should be null, null it out when the count is 0; the `Expr.sum` docstring suggests a `pl.when` guard on the count.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"g": ["a", "a", "b"], "x": [None, None, 5]},
    schema={"g": pl.String, "x": pl.Int64},
)
out = df.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg(
    pl.col("x").sum().alias("naive"),
    pl.col("x").count().alias("n"),
    # max is null when a group has no non-null values, so this nulls empty sums
    (pl.col("x").sum() + pl.col("x").max() * 0).alias("safe"),
)
# group a: naive=0 (misleading), n=0, safe=None
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: Fixed-window rolling stats need a full non-null window by default
passed.trap: For `Expr.rolling_sum`, `Expr.rolling_std`, `Expr.rolling_var` and `Expr.rolling_skew`, `min_samples=None` means `min_samples = window_size`. The first `window_size - 1` rows are therefore null. A single null inside the data also nulls out every window that contains it, not just its own row. The docstrings of `Expr.rolling_sum`, `Expr.rolling_std` and `Expr.rolling_var` note that `min_periods` was renamed `min_samples` in 1.21.0. Pass `min_samples=1` (or another threshold) when partial windows should still produce a value.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, None, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0]})
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("x").rolling_sum(2).alias("default"),
    pl.col("x").rolling_sum(2, min_samples=1).alias("lenient"),
)
# default: None, None, None, 7.0, 9.0
# lenient: 1.0, 1.0, 3.0, 7.0, 9.0
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: Rolling-by windows are right-closed and exclude the left edge
passed.trap: `Expr.rolling_sum_by`, `Expr.rolling_std_by` and `Expr.rolling_var_by` default to `closed='right'`. The window at `t` is therefore `(t - window_size, t]`, so a "2d" window over daily data covers today and yesterday, not three days. Pass `closed='both'` if the left boundary must be included. Unlike the fixed-size variants, these default to `min_samples=1`, and an integer `by` column needs an `'i'` window such as `"2i"`. These methods are marked unstable.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import date

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "d": [date(2024, 1, 1), date(2024, 1, 2), date(2024, 1, 3), date(2024, 1, 4)],
        "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    }
)
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("x").rolling_sum_by("d", "2d").alias("right"),
    pl.col("x").rolling_sum_by("d", "2d", closed="both").alias("both"),
)
# right: 1, 3, 5, 7   both: 1, 3, 6, 9
print(out.select("right", "both").to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: skew defaults to the biased estimator
passed.trap: `Expr.skew` and `Expr.rolling_skew` default to `bias=True`, which gives the biased Fisher-Pearson coefficient g1. pandas `skew` and spreadsheet `SKEW` report the bias-adjusted G1, so ported code silently produces smaller-magnitude numbers. Pass `bias=False` to get the adjusted coefficient.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]})
out = df.select(
    pl.col("a").skew().alias("biased"),
    pl.col("a").skew(bias=False).alias("adjusted"),
)
# biased ~0.343622, adjusted ~0.512241
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: round uses bankers' rounding by default
passed.trap: `Expr.round` defaults to `mode='half_to_even'`, so 0.5 rounds to 0.0 and 2.5 rounds to 2.0. People coming from SQL `ROUND` or spreadsheets expect ties to round away from zero, and that habit gives off-by-one results on exact halves. Pass `mode='half_away_from_zero'` for that behaviour.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -2.5]})
out = df.select(
    pl.col("a").round(0).alias("default"),
    pl.col("a").round(0, mode="half_away_from_zero").alias("away"),
)
# default: 0.0, 2.0, 2.0, -2.0
# away:    1.0, 2.0, 3.0, -3.0
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: Nulls sort first, even when descending
passed.trap: `Expr.sort` and `Expr.sort_by` default to `nulls_last=False`, so nulls come first in both ascending and descending order. pandas places missing values last, so a "sort descending then take the first" pattern returns a null instead of the maximum. Pass `nulls_last=True`. `Expr.sort_by` also defaults to `maintain_order=False`, so ties are not guaranteed to keep their original order unless you set it.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["x", "y", "z"], "score": [None, 5, 7]})
wrong = df.select(
    pl.col("name").sort_by("score", descending=True).first().alias("best"),
    pl.col("score").sort(descending=True).first().alias("top"),
)
right = df.select(
    pl.col("name").sort_by("score", descending=True, nulls_last=True).first().alias("best"),
    pl.col("score").sort(descending=True, nulls_last=True).first().alias("top"),
)
print(wrong.to_dicts())  # best=x, top=None
print(right.to_dicts())  # best=z, top=7

passed.title: top_k output is unordered, and top_k_by uses reverse rather than descending
passed.trap: `Expr.top_k` and `Expr.top_k_by` return the k elements in no guaranteed order, so sort afterwards if you need them ranked. In 1.0.0 the `descending` parameter of `Expr.top_k_by` was renamed `reverse`, so use `reverse=True` to get the k smallest. Non-null values are always preferred over nulls, even with `reverse=True`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["a", "b", "c", "d"], "score": [10, 40, None, 30]})
top = df.select(pl.all().top_k_by("score", 2)).sort("score", descending=True)
low = df.select(pl.all().top_k_by("score", 2, reverse=True)).sort("score")
print(top.to_dicts())  # b 40, d 30
print(low.to_dicts())  # a 10, d 30 (null row c is not chosen)
